1.name: Hydrogen
1.uses: Rocket fuel mixtures (liquid hydrogen), industrial Haber process feedstock, fuel cells, scientific research.
1.natural_occurrence: Primordial and in stars; most abundant element in the universe.
1.history: Recognized as a distinct element in the 18th century; named by Lavoisier. Large-scale production grew with electrolysis and steam-reforming.

1.name: Protium
1.info: Most common hydrogen isotope (no neutrons). Stable.

2.name: Deuterium
2.info: Stable isotope with one neutron. Used in heavy water.
2.uses: Heavy water reactors, isotopic labelling, NMR spectroscopy.

3.name: Tritium
3.natural_occurrence: Produced naturally by cosmic rays in the upper atmosphere; also manufactured.

2.name: Helium
2.uses: Cryogenics (liquid helium), pressurizing and cooling in aerospace, gas chromatography carrier gas.
2.natural_occurrence: Primordial (from Big Bang nucleosynthesis) and produced by radioactive decay in Earth's crust; rare in atmosphere.
2.history: Discovered in the solar spectrum (1868) before being isolated on Earth; major supply from natural gas fields.

3.name: Helium-3
3.natural_occurrence: Very rare on Earth, more common on lunar regolith.

3.name: Lithium
3.uses: Lithium-ion batteries, psychiatric medication (lithium carbonate), aerospace alloys.
3.natural_occurrence: Occurs in trace amounts in most igneous rocks and mineral springs.
3.history: Isolated in 1817; named from Greek 'lithos' (stone). Major industrial production began in the 20th century.

4.name: Beryllium
4.uses: Aerospace alloys, X-ray windows, nuclear moderators.
4.natural_occurrence: Found in beryl and other minerals; uncommon but widely distributed.
4.history: Isolated in 1828. Highly toxic in powdered form; requires careful handling.

5.name: Boron
5.uses: Borosilicate glass, detergents, neutron detection, semiconductors.
5.natural_occurrence: Found in boron minerals like borax and colemanite.
5.history: Discovered in 1808; named from the Arabic 'buraq' (borax).

6.name: Carbon
6.uses: Organic chemistry, fuels, steel production (as a component), carbon-fiber materials, filtration (activated carbon).
6.natural_occurrence: Ubiquitous in living organisms, atmosphere (CO2), minerals (carbonates), and fossil fuels.
6.history: Known since antiquity in forms like charcoal and diamond; modern chemistry clarified allotropes and organic chemistry.

7.name: Nitrogen
7.description: Colorless, odorless diatomic gas; 78% of atmosphere.
7.uses: Fertilizers (Haber-Bosch process), liquid nitrogen (cryogenic), explosives, stainless steel production.
7.natural_occurrence: Dominant gas in Earth's atmosphere; also in nitrate minerals and biological compounds.

8.name: Oxygen
8.uses: Medical oxygen, industrial oxidation processes, steelmaking, rocket oxidizer (LOX).
8.natural_occurrence: Abundant in Earth's atmosphere (~21%) and in oxides and silicates in the crust.
8.history: Isolated in the 18th century by Scheele and Priestley; recognized as an element by Lavoisier.

9.name: Fluorine
9.description: Most reactive of all elements; pale yellow gas.
9.uses: Uranium enrichment (UF6), refrigerants (CFCs, HCFCs), toothpaste (fluoride), various organic compounds.
9.natural_occurrence: Found in fluorite (CaF2) and other fluorine-containing minerals.
9.history: Isolated in 1886; named from Latin 'fluere' (to flow).

10.name: Neon
10.description: Inert noble gas; glows reddish-orange in discharge tubes.
10.uses: Neon signs and lamps, high-voltage indicators, cryogenic applications.
10.natural_occurrence: Trace component of Earth's atmosphere; more abundant in the Sun.

11.name: Sodium
11.description: Soft, silvery metal; highly reactive with water.
11.uses: Salt (NaCl) in chemical industry, sodium hydroxide (caustic), street lamps, metal alloys.
11.natural_occurrence: Widespread as halite (rock salt) and in seawater.
11.history: Known since ancient times; isolated in 1807 by Davy via electrolysis.

12.name: Magnesium
12.description: Lightweight metal; essential for photosynthesis (in chlorophyll).
12.uses: Alloys (aerospace, automotive), magnesium oxide (refractory), medical uses, agricultural supplements.
12.natural_occurrence: Abundant in seawater, minerals (olivine, dolomite), and rocks.
12.history: First isolated in 1808 by Davy. Widely used in 20th century for lightweight applications.

13.name: Aluminum
13.description: Lightweight, silvery metal; highly reactive but forms protective oxide layer.
13.uses: Aerospace (aircraft fuselages), automotive parts, beverage cans, construction, electrical wiring.
13.natural_occurrence: Third most abundant element in Earth's crust (bauxite ore).
13.history: Difficult to isolate; modern smelting via Hall-Héroult process (1886) enabled mass production.

14.name: Silicon
14.description: Metalloid; second most abundant element in crust (as silicates).
14.uses: Semiconductors, solar cells, glass, construction materials, computer chips.
14.natural_occurrence: Found in silicate minerals (quartz, feldspar), sand, and rocks.
14.history: Isolated in 1823; central to electronic revolution via silicon transistors and integrated circuits.

15.name: Phosphorus
15.uses: Fertilizers (phosphate rock), detergents, phosphoric acid, bioluminescence compounds.
15.natural_occurrence: Found in phosphate minerals; essential to all living organisms (DNA, ATP).
15.history: First element isolated from a biological source (urine, 1669).

16.name: Sulfur
16.description: Yellow non-metallic element; essential to amino acids.
16.uses: Sulfuric acid (industrial chemical), rubber vulcanization, fertilizers, medical applications.
16.natural_occurrence: Found in sulfide ore minerals, elemental deposits, and as a component of proteins.
16.history: Known since ancient times; sulfur mining has deep historical roots.

17.name: Chlorine
17.description: Toxic greenish-yellow gas; strong oxidizing agent.
17.uses: Water disinfection, PVC production, chemical synthesis, bleach, sterilization.
17.natural_occurrence: Abundant as chlorides (rock salt, seawater); common in nature.
17.history: Discovered in 1774; recognized as an element in 1810. Industrial chlor-alkali process began in the 19th century.

18.name: Argon
18.description: Inert noble gas; colorless and odorless.
18.uses: Welding and cutting (inert shielding), double-pane windows, cryogenics, lighting.
18.history: Discovered in 1894 via atmospheric fractional distillation.

19.name: Potassium
19.description: Soft, silvery alkali metal; essential electrolyte.
19.uses: Fertilizers (potash), chemical synthesis, medical (electrolyte regulation), glass production.
19.natural_occurrence: Common in minerals and seawater; essential for all living cells.
19.history: First element isolated by electrolysis (by Davy in 1807).

20.name: Calcium
20.description: Alkaline earth metal; essential for bones and teeth.
20.uses: Limestone (construction), cement, calcium carbonate supplements, metallurgy, food fortification.
20.natural_occurrence: Fifth most abundant element; found in limestone, gypsum, and fluorite.
20.history: Known in compounds since ancient times; isolated in 1808 by Davy.

21.name: Scandium
21.uses: Aluminum alloys (aerospace), high-intensity lights, nuclear research.
21.natural_occurrence: Trace element; widely dispersed but never concentrated in ore deposits.

22.name: Titanium
22.uses: Aerospace (aircraft structures), medical implants, pigment (TiO2), catalysts.
22.natural_occurrence: Fourth most abundant metal in crust; found in rutile and ilmenite.
22.history: Isolated in 1825; industrial production expanded in the 20th century for aerospace.

23.name: Vanadium
23.uses: Steel alloys, catalysts, vanadium redox batteries, pigments.
23.natural_occurrence: Found in many minerals; trace element in oils.
23.history: Discovered in 1801; industrial use grew with steel production.

24.name: Chromium
24.description: Transition metal; resistant to corrosion; essential trace element.
24.uses: Stainless steel, chromium plating, pigments (chrome yellow), catalysts.
24.natural_occurrence: Found in chromite ore; trace nutrient for glucose metabolism.
24.history: Discovered in 1797; chromium plating became widespread in 20th century.

25.name: Manganese
25.uses: Steel alloys, batteries, manganese dioxide (oxidizer), water treatment, trace nutrient.
25.natural_occurrence: Found in manganese nodules on ocean floor and terrestrial deposits.
25.history: Known since ancient times (black oxide); became important in steel industry.

26.name: Iron
26.uses: Construction (steel), manufacturing, catalysts, hemoglobin in biology.
26.natural_occurrence: Abundant in Earth's crust and core; meteorites commonly contain iron-nickel alloys.
26.history: Used since the Iron Age; smelting technology enabled large-scale use.

27.name: Cobalt
27.description: Transition metal; ferromagnetic; essential trace element.
27.uses: High-strength alloys, pigments (cobalt blue), catalysts, batteries, magnetic applications.
27.natural_occurrence: Found in cobaltite and other ores; trace nutrient (vitamin B12).
27.history: Used for blue pigments since medieval times; modern applications expanded in 20th century.

28.name: Nickel
28.uses: Stainless steel, plating, batteries, catalysts, coinage metals.
28.natural_occurrence: Found in laterite and sulfide ores; also in Earth's core (iron-nickel).
28.history: Known since ancient times in meteorites; industrial production began in the 18th century.

29.name: Copper
29.description: Transition metal; excellent electrical and thermal conductor; reddish color.
29.uses: Electrical wiring, plumbing, alloys (brass, bronze), antimicrobial coatings, catalysts.
29.natural_occurrence: Native copper found in some deposits; also in chalcopyrite and other sulfides.
29.history: One of the earliest metals used by humans (Bronze Age); widely traded in antiquity.

30.name: Zinc
30.description: Transition metal; bluish-white; essential trace element.
30.uses: Galvanized steel (corrosion protection), brass alloys, die-casting, nutritional supplement.
30.natural_occurrence: Found in sphalerite and calamine ores; trace nutrient for human health.
30.history: Known in ancient brass; isolated as an element in 1746.

31.name: Gallium
31.description: Soft metal; liquid near room temperature.
31.uses: Semiconductors (integrated circuits, LEDs), photovoltaic solar cells, optoelectronics.
31.natural_occurrence: Trace element in aluminum ores and zinc blende; no concentrated ore.
31.history: Predicted by Mendeleev; discovered in 1875. Critical for modern electronics.

32.name: Germanium
32.uses: Semiconductors, fiber optics, infrared optics, integrated circuits.
32.natural_occurrence: Trace element in coal, zinc ores, and other minerals.
32.history: Confirmed Mendeleev's prediction; discovered in 1886. Important for transistor development.

33.name: Arsenic
33.natural_occurrence: Found in sulfide minerals; contaminant in some ore deposits and groundwater.
33.history: Known since ancient times; famous as a poison in medieval Europe.

34.name: Selenium
34.uses: Photocells, xerography, glass decolorizer, nutritional supplement, solar cells.
34.natural_occurrence: Trace element in rocks and soils; essential for selenoproteins.
34.history: Discovered in 1817; modern applications exploit its photoelectric properties.

35.name: Bromine
35.uses: Flame retardants, organobromine pharmaceuticals, water disinfection, photography.
35.natural_occurrence: Found in seawater as bromide; also in mineral brines.
35.history: Discovered in 1826; extracted from seawater on large scale.

36.name: Krypton
36.uses: High-efficiency lightbulbs, laser systems, filling double-pane windows.
36.history: Discovered in 1898 via atmospheric fractional distillation.

37.name: Rubidium
37.uses: Atomic clocks, photomultiplier tubes, ion engines, research applications.
37.natural_occurrence: Trace element in minerals and rocks; widely dispersed.
37.history: Discovered spectroscopically in 1861; one of the first elements discovered by spectroscopy.

38.name: Strontium
38.uses: Fireworks (red color), television tubes, medical radioisotopes, bone analogs.
38.natural_occurrence: Found in strontianite and celestite minerals.
38.history: Named after Strontian, Scotland. Sr-90 is a significant radioactive fallout product.

39.name: Yttrium
39.natural_occurrence: Found in rare earth minerals like xenotime and monazite.
39.history: Discovered in 1794 as part of a rare earth mineral.

40.name: Zirconium
40.description: Transition metal; corrosion-resistant; used in nuclear reactors.
40.uses: Nuclear fuel cladding, ceramics, refractory materials, jewelry (cubic zirconia).
40.natural_occurrence: Found in zircon (ZrSiO4) and baddeleyite; one of the more abundant transition metals.
40.history: Isolated in pure form in 1824; large-scale use began in nuclear industry.

41.name: Niobium
41.uses: Superconductive alloys, high-strength steel alloys, superconducting magnets.
41.natural_occurrence: Found in columbite and pyrochlore minerals.
41.history: Isolated in 1801; named from Niobe in Greek mythology.

42.name: Molybdenum
42.natural_occurrence: Found in molybdenite; widely dispersed trace element.
42.history: Discovered in 1778; became important for high-temperature alloys.

43.name: Technetium
43.natural_occurrence: Not found in nature; produced synthetically in nuclear reactors.
43.history: First element synthesized artificially (1937); named from Greek 'technetos' (artificial).

44.name: Ruthenium
44.description: Transition metal; rare; hard and resistant to corrosion.
44.uses: Platinum alloys, catalysts, electronics, wear-resistant compounds.
44.natural_occurrence: Found in platinum ores and as native ruthenium.
44.history: Discovered in 1844; extracted from platinum ore residues.

45.name: Rhodium
45.description: Transition metal; rare; highly resistant to corrosion.
45.uses: Catalytic converters (automobile), jewelry alloys, reflective coatings.
45.natural_occurrence: Found in platinum ores; one of the rarest elements.
45.history: Discovered in 1803; expensive and valuable for catalytic applications.

46.name: Palladium
46.uses: Catalytic converters, jewelry alloys, hydrogen absorption (storage), electronics.
46.natural_occurrence: Found in platinum ores; also alloyed with gold in some deposits.
46.history: Discovered in 1803; critical for environmental catalysis.

47.name: Silver
47.description: Transition metal; precious metal; excellent conductor.
47.uses: Jewelry, photography (historical), electronics, antibacterial coatings, solar panels.
47.natural_occurrence: Found as native silver and in sulfide minerals; secondary product of copper and lead mining.
47.history: Known since ancient times; used for currency and precious items.

48.name: Cadmium
48.uses: Batteries, pigments (historic), nuclear control rods, plating.
48.natural_occurrence: Found as a trace element in zinc ores; environmental contaminant.
48.history: Discovered in 1817; widely used in batteries and plating before toxicity concerns.

49.name: Indium
49.description: Soft metal; rare; excellent semiconductor properties.
49.uses: Semiconductors, photovoltaic cells (indium tin oxide), liquid crystal displays (LCDs).
49.natural_occurrence: Trace element in zinc ores; no concentrated ore deposits.
49.history: Discovered spectroscopically in 1863. Modern demand driven by LCD and solar industries.

50.name: Tin
50.uses: Solder, tin cans (tin-plated steel), alloys (bronze, pewter), integrated circuits.
50.natural_occurrence: Found in cassiterite ore; historically mined in Cornwall and Southeast Asia.
50.history: One of the earliest metals used (Bronze Age); essential for alloy production.

51.name: Antimony
51.natural_occurrence: Found in stibnite ore and as native antimony.
51.history: Known since ancient times; used as a medicine in medieval alchemy.

52.name: Tellurium
52.natural_occurrence: Rare; found in gold and copper ores.
52.history: Discovered in 1782; relatively uncommon in Earth's crust.

53.name: Iodine
53.description: Halogen; essential trace element; bluish-black solid.
53.uses: Nutritional supplements (iodized salt), disinfectants, contrast media (medical imaging), pharmaceutical compounds.
53.natural_occurrence: Found in iodine-rich minerals and seawater; essential for thyroid function.
53.history: Discovered in seaweed in 1811; important public health element.

54.name: Xenon
54.description: Noble gas; colorless, odorless; anesthetic properties.
54.uses: High-intensity discharge lamps, anesthesia, ion propulsion drives, research.

55.name: Cesium
55.description: Soft alkali metal; highly reactive; golden color.
55.uses: Atomic clocks (defining the second), photoelectric cells, ion engines.
55.natural_occurrence: Trace element; found in minerals and distributed in the environment.
55.history: First element discovered by spectroscopy (1860); critical for precise timekeeping.

56.name: Barium
56.uses: Barium sulfate (medical X-ray contrast), barium carbonate (glass), drilling fluids.
56.natural_occurrence: Found in barite and witherite minerals.
56.history: Known since ancient times; isolated in 1808.

57.name: Lanthanum
57.uses: Catalytic converters, optical glasses, hydrogen storage alloys.
57.natural_occurrence: Found in rare earth minerals; relatively abundant rare earth.
57.history: Discovered in 1839; first of the lanthanide series.

58.name: Cerium
58.description: Rare earth element; most abundant lanthanide.
58.uses: Catalytic converters (automobile), polishing powders, high-temperature alloys.
58.natural_occurrence: Found in monazite and bastnäsite; most abundant rare earth element.
58.history: Discovered in 1803; important for catalytic applications.

59.name: Praseodymium
59.uses: Magnets, lamps, catalysts, green glass colorant.
59.history: Separated from cerium in 1885; important for high-performance magnets.

60.name: Neodymium
60.description: Rare earth element; forms powerful magnets.
60.uses: Neodymium magnets (high-performance), lasers, lamps, optical glass.
60.natural_occurrence: Found in rare earth minerals; second most abundant rare earth.
60.history: Discovered in 1885; critical for modern magnets and clean energy.

61.name: Promethium
61.description: Rare earth element; radioactive (no stable isotopes).
61.uses: Beta radiation sources, luminous paint, atomic batteries.
61.natural_occurrence: Not found in nature; produced in nuclear reactors.
61.history: Last element to be discovered/isolated (1945); named after Prometheus.

62.name: Samarium
62.uses: Samarium-cobalt magnets, nuclear control rods, catalysts.
62.history: Discovered in 1879; important for high-temperature magnets.

63.name: Europium
63.uses: Red phosphors (CRT and LCD displays), lighting, medical applications.
63.natural_occurrence: Found in rare earth minerals and in seawater.
63.history: Discovered in 1896; critical for color displays.

64.name: Gadolinium
64.uses: MRI contrast agents, neutron absorption (nuclear control), high-temperature alloys.
64.history: Discovered in 1880; essential for medical imaging.

65.name: Terbium
65.history: Discovered in 1843; important for modern display technology.

66.name: Dysprosium
66.uses: Magnets, nuclear control rods, optical devices.
66.history: Discovered in 1886; important for high-temperature applications.

67.name: Holmium
67.uses: Magnets, nuclear control rods, medical lasers.
67.history: Discovered in 1879; minor role in modern technology.

68.name: Erbium
68.uses: Fiber optics (amplifiers), nuclear control rods, catalysts.

69.name: Thulium
69.uses: Portable X-ray devices, nuclear control rods, catalysts.
69.natural_occurrence: Found in rare earth minerals; extremely rare.
69.history: Discovered in 1879; niche applications due to scarcity.

70.name: Ytterbium
70.uses: Atomic clocks, stainless steel improvement, catalysts.
70.history: Discovered in 1878; emerging applications in precision timekeeping.

71.name: Lutetium
71.description: Rare earth element; last of the lanthanides.
71.uses: Positron emission tomography (PET), catalysts, nuclear control rods.
71.natural_occurrence: Found in rare earth minerals; rarest lanthanide.
71.history: Last stable lanthanide discovered (1907); rare earth series complete.

72.name: Hafnium
72.description: Transition metal; high melting point; neutron absorber.
72.uses: Nuclear reactor control rods, refractory materials, high-temperature ceramics.
72.natural_occurrence: Found in zircon alongside zirconium; difficult to separate.
72.history: Isolated in 1923; important for nuclear safety.

73.name: Tantalum
73.description: Transition metal; rare; highly resistant to corrosion.
73.uses: Electronics (capacitors), surgical implants, high-temperature alloys, catalysts.
73.natural_occurrence: Found in tantalite ore; conflict mineral concerns in certain regions.
73.history: Discovered in 1802; demand driven by electronics industry.

74.name: Tungsten
74.description: Transition metal; highest melting point of all metals.
74.uses: Light bulb filaments, high-temperature alloys, catalysts, X-ray targets.
74.natural_occurrence: Found in wolframite and scheelite ores.
74.history: Isolated in 1783; critical for high-temperature applications.

75.name: Rhenium
75.description: Transition metal; rare; high density; high melting point.
75.uses: High-temperature superalloys (jet engines), catalysts, thermoelectric devices.
75.natural_occurrence: Trace element; extracted from molybdenum ore processing.
75.history: Last stable element to be discovered (1925); critical for aerospace.

76.name: Osmium
76.uses: Osmium alloys (fountain pens, surgical instruments), catalysts, osmium tetroxide.
76.natural_occurrence: Found in platinum ores; rarest precious metal.
76.history: Discovered in 1803; extremely rare and expensive.

77.name: Iridium
77.uses: Jewelry alloys, crucibles (high-temperature chemistry), catalysts, surgical instruments.
77.natural_occurrence: Found in platinum ores; one of the rarest elements.
77.history: Discovered in 1803; used in precision instruments and jewelry.

78.name: Platinum
78.uses: Catalytic converters, jewelry, laboratory equipment, cancer drugs (cisplatin).
78.natural_occurrence: Found as native platinum in certain deposits; secondary from copper and nickel mining.
78.history: Known to ancient cultures; major supply from South Africa and Russia.

79.name: Gold
79.description: Precious transition metal; highly unreactive; golden color.
79.natural_occurrence: Found as native gold in hydrothermal veins and placer deposits; often with other metals.
79.history: One of the first metals used by humans; symbol of wealth since antiquity.

80.name: Mercury
80.description: Transition metal; liquid at room temperature.
80.uses: Historical: thermometers, barometers; Current: fluorescent lamps, dental amalgam.
80.natural_occurrence: Found in cinnabar ore; volatile and widely dispersed as a contaminant.
80.history: Known since ancient times; highly toxic; use increasingly restricted.

81.name: Thallium
81.uses: Optical materials, semiconductors, photomultiplier tubes, historical rodenticide (now banned).
81.natural_occurrence: Trace element; found in certain ores and as a contaminant.
81.history: Discovered spectroscopically in 1861; toxic at low levels.

82.name: Lead
82.uses: Batteries, radiation shielding (X-ray, nuclear), pigments (lead paint—now restricted), solder.
82.natural_occurrence: Found in galena ore; widely dispersed; major environmental contaminant.
82.history: Used since ancient times for water pipes (now understood to cause lead poisoning).

83.name: Bismuth
83.description: Post-transition metal; brittle; low toxicity (compared to lead).
83.uses: Bismuth oxide (catalysts), pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, nuclear control rods.
83.natural_occurrence: Found as native bismuth and in sulfide ores; secondary product.
83.history: Known since medieval times; safer alternative to lead in some applications.

84.name: Polonium
84.uses: Static eliminators, heat sources for spacecraft, research.
84.natural_occurrence: Trace element from U-238 decay chain; extremely rare in nature.
84.history: Discovered by Marie Curie in 1898; named after Poland.

85.name: Astatine
85.uses: Medical research (potential cancer treatment), tracer studies.
85.natural_occurrence: Produced naturally by radioactive decay; only trace amounts exist.

86.name: Radon
86.uses: Medical research, radon therapy (disputed), geological research.
86.natural_occurrence: Produced by uranium decay in soil and rocks; accumulates in buildings (health concern).
86.history: Discovered in 1900; significant indoor air pollutant.

87.name: Francium
87.description: Alkali metal; highly reactive; radioactive; extremely rare.
87.natural_occurrence: Rarest element; only trace amounts from U-235 decay.
87.history: Discovered in 1939; only a few atoms ever produced.

88.name: Radium
88.uses: Medical research (radiotherapy), historical luminous paints (now restricted).
88.natural_occurrence: Produced by uranium and thorium decay; extremely rare.
88.history: Discovered by Curies in 1898; historical use as medicine (now understood to be toxic).

89.name: Actinium
89.uses: Neutron source (Ac-227), medical research, nuclear research.
89.natural_occurrence: Trace amounts from uranium decay; produced in reactors.
89.history: Discovered in 1899; important for nuclear physics research.

90.name: Thorium
90.uses: Nuclear fuel (proposed), ceramics, welding rods, catalysts.
90.natural_occurrence: Found in monazite and other rare earth minerals; more abundant than uranium.
90.history: Known since 1828; considered for nuclear power.

91.name: Protactinium
91.uses: Nuclear research, isotope production, research applications.
91.natural_occurrence: Trace amounts from uranium decay; extremely rare.

92.name: Uranium
92.uses: Nuclear fuel, nuclear weapons, depleted uranium (kinetic energy weapons), medical imaging.
92.natural_occurrence: Found in uranite and other minerals; alpha emitter.
92.history: Discovered in 1789; central to nuclear energy and arms issues.

93.name: Neptunium
93.uses: Nuclear research, heat sources, detection instruments.
93.natural_occurrence: Produced in nuclear reactors; trace amounts from U-237 decay.
93.history: First transuranium element (1940); named after planet Neptune.

94.name: Plutonium
94.uses: Nuclear weapons, nuclear fuel, heat sources (space missions), research.
94.natural_occurrence: Produced in nuclear reactors; trace amounts from U-238 bombardment.
94.history: Synthesized in 1940; critical for nuclear weapons and energy.

95.name: Americium
95.uses: Smoke detectors, radiography, neutron sources, medical research.
95.natural_occurrence: Produced in nuclear reactors; Am-241 from Pu-241 decay.
95.history: Synthesized in 1944; widely used in household smoke detectors.

96.name: Curium
96.uses: Heat sources for space probes, radiotherapy research, neutron sources.
96.history: Synthesized in 1944; named after Marie and Pierre Curie.

97.name: Berkelium
97.uses: Nuclear research, neutron sources, production of other elements.
97.history: Synthesized in 1949; named after Berkeley, California.

98.name: Californium
98.uses: Neutron sources (medical, industrial), nuclear weapons research, oil well logging.

99.name: Einsteinium
99.uses: Nuclear research, production of other heavy elements.
99.natural_occurrence: Produced only in nuclear reactors or from thermonuclear explosions.
99.history: Synthesized in 1952 during H-bomb test; named after Einstein.

100.name: Fermium
100.uses: Nuclear physics research, exotic isotope production.
100.history: Synthesized in 1952; named after Enrico Fermi.

101.name: Mendelevium
101.history: Synthesized in 1955; named after Dmitri Mendeleev.

102.name: Nobelium
102.history: Synthesized in 1958; named after Alfred Nobel.

103.name: Lawrencium
103.history: Synthesized in 1961; named after Ernest Lawrence.

104.name: Rutherfordium
104.history: Synthesized in 1969; named after Ernest Rutherford.

105.name: Dubnium
105.history: Synthesized in 1970; named after Dubna, Russia.

106.name: Seaborgium
106.history: Synthesized in 1974; named after Glenn T. Seaborg.

107.name: Bohrium
107.history: Synthesized in 1981; named after Niels Bohr.

108.name: Hassium
108.history: Synthesized in 1984; named after Hesse, Germany.

109.name: Meitnerium
109.history: Synthesized in 1982; named after Lise Meitner.

110.name: Darmstadtium
110.history: Synthesized in 1994; named after Darmstadt, Germany.

111.name: Roentgenium
111.history: Synthesized in 1994; named after Wilhelm Röntgen.

112.name: Copernicium
112.history: Synthesized in 1996; named after Nicolaus Copernicus.

114.name: Flerovium
114.history: Synthesized in 1998; named after Flerov, Russia.

116.name: Livermorium
116.history: Synthesized in 2000; named after Livermore, California.

118.name: Oganesson
118.description: Noble gas; radioactive; extremely rare; superheavy element.
118.history: Synthesized in 2006; newest element; named after Yuri Oganessian.
